rules.quote: Singular pronouns have a gender-neutral form. Use the forms:
rules.specification: Interpret this as guidance for gender-neutral singular references, not a prohibition on all gendered pronouns. The listed substitutions are they for he or she, them for him or her, and their for his or hers.
rules.violation_condition: A gendered singular pronoun is used where a gender-neutral reference is intended, instead of the corresponding form ‘they’, ‘them’ or ‘their’.
when: The singular reference is intended to be gender-neutral.
The replacement form depends on the pronoun’s grammatical function.
rules.why: G-2 combines the case-dependent substitutions into one gender-neutral-form check; the scope interpretation is explicit.

rules.quote: When the singular ‘they’ is used in a sentence as a gender-neutral term, it takes the plural form of a verb.
rules.violation_condition: Gender-neutral singular ‘they’ takes a singular verb form where the singular and plural forms differ.
when: ‘They’ refers to a singular person as a gender-neutral term.
The verb has distinct singular and plural forms.
rules.why: This states a checkable verb-agreement requirement distinct from pronoun case and pronoun selection.

covers.quote: A pronoun used as the subject in a sentence is in the subjective case (for example, ‘I’, ‘they’).
A pronoun used as the object in a sentence is in the objective case (for example, ‘me’, ‘them’).

examples.note: Subjective ‘I’ and objective ‘them’.

parts.quote: I emailed them.

examples.note: Subjective ‘They’ and objective ‘me’.

parts.quote: They emailed me.

examples.note: The pronoun is part of the subject.

parts.quote: My colleague and I travelled with the delegation.

examples.note: The pronoun is part of the object.

parts.quote: My manager sent their director and me an email.

examples.note: Objective ‘me’ is used in the subject.

parts.quote: My colleague and me travelled with the delegation.

examples.note: Subjective ‘I’ is used in the object.

parts.quote: My manager sent their director and I an email.

rules.quote: Use the correct case when writing pronouns.
rules.violation_condition: A non-reflexive pronoun used as a verb’s subject has objective case, or one used as the verb’s object has subjective case.
when: The pronoun functions as the subject or object of a verb.
The check also applies when the pronoun is coordinated with another subject or object.
Reflexive-pronoun misuse is covered by the separate reflexive-pronoun rules.
rules.why: G-2 keeps subject and object cases together; G-4 uses the actionable body instruction rather than the descriptive heading.

covers.quote: Sentences can have reflexive pronouns when the subject is also the object of the verb.

examples.note: The reflexive object refers to the subject.

parts.quote: The manager emailed themself.

examples.note: The subject and object refer to the same person.

parts.quote: I emailed myself.

examples.note: The reflexive object does not refer to the subject.

parts.quote: The manager emailed myself.

rules.quote: Don’t use a reflexive pronoun if the subject and the object are not the same person or thing.
rules.violation_condition: A reflexive pronoun used as a verb’s object refers to a different person or thing from that verb’s subject.
when: A reflexive pronoun functions as the object of a verb.
A reflexive object is permitted when it refers to the same person or thing as the subject.
rules.why: G-3 records the permission as the allowed condition, not as an additional rule; E-2 attaches the nearest examples.

examples.note: The subject uses a subjective personal pronoun.

parts.quote: My colleague and I travelled with the delegation.

examples.note: A reflexive pronoun is part of the subject.

parts.quote: My colleague and myself travelled with the delegation.

rules.quote: Don’t use reflexive pronouns such as ‘yourself’ and ‘myself’ as the subject of the verb.
rules.violation_condition: A reflexive pronoun functions as all or part of a verb’s subject.
when: The reflexive pronoun functions as a subject, including within a coordinated subject.
rules.why: The subject-position violation is distinct from a reflexive object referring to the wrong person; E-2 keeps its contrast pair here.

covers.quote: Choosing between relative pronouns can be a matter of style in some situations, depending on voice and tone.

examples.note: The relative clause supplies essential identifying information.

parts.quote: The farm that produces oats is for sale.

examples.note: The relative clause supplies non-essential information.

parts.quote: The farm, which produces oats, is for sale.

rules.quote: To make your writing clear, use:
rules.specification: Prefer ‘that’ for essential information and ‘which’ for non-essential information. The page allows other choices depending on voice and tone but does not define when those exceptions apply. Punctuation is checked separately.
rules.violation_condition: When choosing between ‘that’ and ‘which’ as relative pronouns, ‘which’ introduces essential information or ‘that’ introduces non-essential information, contrary to the preferred distinction and without an applicable voice or tone exception.
when: The choice is between ‘that’ and ‘which’ as relative pronouns.
Pronoun choice can vary with voice and tone in some situations; the page leaves those situations unspecified.
rules.why: G-2 combines the two information-status cases; G-3 preserves the style exception; E-1 treats both contrasting examples as compliant.

covers.quote: It is the use of punctuation with the relative pronoun that clarifies meaning.

examples.note: Commas separate the non-essential relative clause.

parts.quote: The farm, which produces oats, is for sale.

rules.quote: It is important to show users whether information is essential or non-essential by using punctuation, for example commas.
rules.violation_condition: A non-essential relative clause lacks punctuation separating it from the main clause.
when: The relative clause supplies non-essential information.
Commas are an example of suitable punctuation, not the only permitted punctuation.
rules.why: Missing punctuation is a different finding from relative-pronoun choice; G-4 absorbs the repeated punctuation guidance.
